{{short description|British theoretical chemist and computer scientist}}
{{EngvarB|date=September 2014}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=December 2019}}{{cleanup|reason=Citations are formatted incorrectly per MOS (page ranges, italics, quote marks, punctuation around author initials).|date=October 2020}}
'''Michael Peter Barnett''' (24 March 1929 – 13 March 2012) was a British [[theoretical chemist]] and [[computer scientist]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.physicstoday.org/1.2753400 |title=Obituary of Michael Barnett (1929–2012) |publisher=Physics Today |accessdate=4 May 2012 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://archive.today/20120906194026/http://www.physicstoday.org/1.2753400 |archivedate=6 September 2012}}</ref> He developed mathematical and computer techniques for [[Quantum chemistry|quantum chemical]] problems, and some of the earliest software for several other kinds of computer application. After his early days in London, Essex and Lancashire, he went to [[King's College, London]], in 1945, the [[Royal Radar Establishment]] in Malvern in 1953, [[IBM]] United Kingdom in 1955, the [[University of Wisconsin]] Department of Chemistry in 1957, and the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] [[John C. Slater#The Solid State and Molecular Theory Group|Solid State and Molecular Theory Group]] in 1958.

At MIT he was an associate professor of physics and director of the [[John C. Slater#Slater's further activities at MIT during this time|Cooperative Computing Laboratory]]. He returned to England, to the [[Institute of Computer Science]] of the [[University of London]] in 1964, and then back to United States the following year. He worked in industry, and taught at [[Columbia University]] 1975–77 and [[Brooklyn College, City University of New York]], 1977–96, retiring as an emeritus professor. After retirement he focused on [[symbolic calculation]] in [[quantum chemistry]] and [[nuclear magnetic resonance]].

==Early life and career==
Barnett spent most of the World War II years near [[Fleetwood]] in Lancashire. He attended [[Baines School|Baines' Grammar School]] in [[Poulton-le-Fylde]], then went to [[King's College, London]] in 1945, where he received a BSc in chemistry in 1948, a PhD for work in the theoretical physics department with [[Charles Coulson]] in 1952, that he continued on a one-year post-doctoral fellowship. His assigned project was to determine if [[electrostatic forces]] could account for the energy needed to make two parts of an [[ethane]] molecule rotate around the bond that joins them.<ref name=mpbPhD>Michael Peter Barnett, ''The Evaluation of Integrals Occurring in the theory of molecular structure''. PhD thesis, University of London, 1952.</ref>

This work required the evaluation of certain mathematical objects – molecular integrals over [[Slater orbitals]]. Barnett extended some earlier work by [[Charles Coulson]]<ref>Charles A Coulson, ''The evaluation of certain integrals occurring in the theory of molecular structure'', Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society, 33, 104, 1937.</ref> by discovering some [[recurrence relation|recurrence formulas]],<ref name=mpbPhD /><ref>Michael P Barnett and Charles A Coulson, Evaluation of integrals occurring in the theory of molecular structure, Part I: Basic Functions, Phil. Trans. Royal Society (London) A 243, pages 221–233, 1951.</ref><ref>Michael P Barnett and Charles A Coulson, Evaluation of integrals occurring in the theory of molecular structure, Part II: Overlap, resonance, Coulomb, hybrid and other two-centre integrals, Phil. Trans. Royal Society (London) A 243, pages 234–249, 1951.</ref> that are part of a method of analysis and computation frequently referred to as the Barnett-Coulson expansion.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20110722185435/http://oai.dtic.mil/oai/oai?verb=getRecord&metadataPrefix=html&identifier=AD0640389 M J M Bernal and J M Mills, ''Evaluation of molecular integrals by the method of Barnett and Coulson'', DTC online, ''Information for the Defense Community'', 1960.]</ref><ref>John C Slater, ''Quantum Theory of Matter'', McGraw-Hill 1968, pages 543–545.</ref> Molecular integrals remain a significant problem in quantum chemistry<ref>Hassan Safouhi and Ahmed Bouferguene, ''Computational chemistry'', in Mohamed Medhat Gaber, ''Scientific Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery: Principles and Foundations'', Springer, New York, 2010. {{ISBN|978-3-642-02787-1}}, e-{{ISBN|978-3-642-02788-8}}. page 173.</ref> and continued to be one of Barnett's main interests.<ref>Michael P Barnett, ''Chemical calculations and chemicals that might calculate'', International Journal of Quantum Chemistry, 109, 1640–1657, 2009.</ref>

Two years after Barnett started this work, he was invited to be one of the twenty-five participants in a conference that was organised by [[Robert Mulliken]], sponsored by the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]] and known, from its venue, as the [[Shelter Island Conference on Quantum Mechanics in Valence Theory, 1951|Shelter Island Conference on Quantum Mechanics in Valence Theory]].<ref>Robert G Parr and Bryce L Crawford. ''National Academy of Sciences Conference on Quantum-Mechanical Methods in Valence Theory'', Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 38, pages 547–554, 1952.</ref><ref>R.G. Parr, ''The Genesis of a Theory'', International Journal of Quantum Chemistry, 37, pages 327–347, 1996.</ref> Barnett's attendance was enabled by the [[British Rayon Research Association]], which supported his post-graduate work.<ref>C A Coulson and M P Barnett, ''The evaluation of unit molecular integrals'', Proceedings of the Shelter Island conference "Quantum Mechanics in Valence Theory", pages 237–271, Office of Naval Research, Washington, DC. 1951 – see Acknowledgements.</ref>

At the [[Royal Radar Establishment]], Barnett held a Senior Government Fellowship. He worked on aspects of theoretical [[solid state physics]], that included the properties of [[organic semiconductor]]s.<ref>M P Barnett (ed), ''Band Structure: Theory and Experiment''. Proceedings of a Symposium Held at RRE Malvern on 27 and 28 September 1954.</ref> As part of his work at IBM United Kingdom, he directed an [[IBM 650|IBM model 650]] computer centre. He directed and participated in numerous projects that included (1) calculating [[DNA]] structures from crystallographic data,<ref>R. W. Langridge, M. P. Barnett and A. F. Mann, ''Calculation of the Fourier transform of a helical molecule'', Journal of Molecular Biology, 2, 63, 1960.</ref> and (2) simulations to plan the location and operation of dams and reservoirs on the [[River Nile]], working with Humphry Morrice, the hydrological advisor to the Government of the Sudan, and his predecessor, Nimmo Allen.<ref>H.A.W. Morrice and W N Allan, ''Planning for the ultimate hydraulic development of the Nile Valley'', Proceedings of the Institute of Civil Engineers, 14, 101, 1959.</ref><ref>M P Barnett, ''Comment on the Nile Valley Calculations'', Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, volume 19, 223, 1957.</ref>

In 1957, Barnett accepted an invitation from [[Joseph Hirschfelder]],<ref>[http://www.nap.edu/openbook.php?record_id=4961& R.B. Bird, C.F. Curtiss and P.R. Certain, ''Joseph Oakland Hirschfelder, May 27, 1911 – March 30, 1990'', Biographical Memoirs, 66, pages 190–205, 1995, The National Academies Press, Washington, D.C.]</ref> in the Chemistry department of the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]], to work on mathematical theories of [[combustion]] and [[detonation]].<ref>C. F. Curtiss, J. O. Hirschfelder and M P Barnett, ''Theory of detonations, Part III: Ignition temperature approximation'', Journal of Chemical Physics, 30, 470, 1959.</ref>

==Activities at MIT==
In 1958, [[John Clarke Slater]] invited Barnett to join his [[John C. Slater#The Solid State and Molecular Theory Group|Solid State and Molecular Theory Group]]. He was made an associate professor of physics in 1960 and, in 1962, set up an [[IBM 709]] installation, the [[John C. Slater#Slater's further activities at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology during this time|Cooperative Computing Laboratory]] (CCL). This supported heavy computations by several groups at MIT.<ref name=presidentsReport>{{Cite web |url=http://libraries.mit.edu/archives/mithistory/presidents-reports/1963.pdf |title=Michael P Barnett, "Cooperative Computing Laboratory", pages 336–7, in ''President's Report Issue 1963''. Massachusetts Institute of Technology Bulletin, volume 99, number 2, November, 1963. |access-date=18 February 2011 |archive-date=5 March 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160305075006/http://libraries.mit.edu/archives/mithistory/presidents-reports/1963.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> The SSMTG used much of the time for molecular and solid state research, attracting many post-doctoral workers from the United Kingdom and Canada,.<ref name=sutcliffe>[https://books.google.com/books?id=FmL-DYjIuP0C&q=Barnett+CoulsonBrian&pg=PA283 T. Sutcliffe, ''The development of computational chemistry in the United Kingdom'', page 283, in Kenneth B. Lipkowitz and Donald B. Boyd (eds.), ''Reviews in Computational Chemistry'', vol. 10, Wiley, 2003.] {{ISBN|978-0-471-18648-9}} {{issn|1069-3599}}</ref>

The calculations of quantum chemistry involve approximate solutions of the Schrödinger equation. Many methods for computing these require molecular integrals that are defined for systems of 2, 3 and 4 atoms, respectively. The 4-atom (or 4-centre) integrals are by far the most difficult. By extending the methods of his PhD papers, Barnett developed a detailed methodology for evaluating all of these integrals<ref>M P Barnett, ''The evaluation of molecular integrals by the zeta—function method'', in ''Methods in computational physics'', volume 2, ''Quantum Mechanics'', ed. B Alder, S Fernbach and M Rotenberg, pages 95–153, Academic Press, New York, 1963.</ref> These were coded in [[FORTRAN]], in software that was available to the IBM mainframe community through the SHARE organisation.<ref name=sutcliffe /> Members of the SSMTG who developed and used these programs included Donald Ellis,<ref>[http://www.physics.northwestern.edu/people/personalpages/dellis.html Donald Ellis, Department of Physics and Astronomy, North Western University] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110720014207/http://www.physics.northwestern.edu/people/personalpages/dellis.html |date=20 July 2011}}</ref> [[Russell M. Pitzer|Russell Pitzer]] and [[Donald Merrifield]].

In 1960, Barnett started to extend a technique he had learned from [[S. Francis Boys|Frank Boys]] to program a computer to construct coded mathematical formulas.<ref>S F Boys, G B Cook, C M Reeves and I Shavitt, Nature, 178, 1207–9, 1956.</ref> He needed a way to typeset these. A [[Phototypesetting|Photon]] machine, equipped with paper provided an immediate solution. Barnett developed software to typeset computer output, and applied this to documents containing mathematical formulas and to a wide range of other typesetting problems. He produced books for the [[MIT Libraries]],<ref>B.P.N. Shih, R.L. Snyder, M.P. Barnett and D.A. Luce, ''Union list of Chinese communist periodicals'', MIT Libraries, Cambridge, Massachusetts, 1963.</ref> and with [[Izs·k|Imre Izs·k]], the [[Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory]].<ref>I.G. Izsak, J.M. Gerard, R. Efimba and M.P. Barnett, ''Construction of Newcomb operators on a digital computer'', Research in Space Science Special Report Number 140, Smithsonian Institution Astrophysical Observatory, Cambridge, Massachusetts, 1964.</ref> The work of his team and the parallel work of other groups through 1964 is described in his monograph.<ref name=mitPress>M.P. Barnett, ''Computer Typesetting, Experiments and Prospects'', MIT Press, 1965.</ref>

Barnett also began to develop his ideas on cognitive modelling, as a member of [[Francis O. Schmitt|Frank Schmitt]]'s seminar on biological memory.<ref>M.P. Barnett, ''Some comments suggested by a consideration of computers'', in ''Macromolecular specificity and biological memory'', ed. F.O. Schmidt, pages 24–27, MIT Press, Cambridge, 1962.</ref> He wrote on river simulation<ref>D.F Manzer and M.P. Barnett, ''Analysis by Simulation: Programming techniques for a High-Speed Digital Computer'', in Arthur Maas et al., ''Design of Water Resource Systems'', pages 324–390, Harvard University Press, Cambridge, Massachusetts, 1962.</ref> as a member of the Harvard Water Resources seminar (see [[Robert Dorfman#Work and Professional opinions|for related work]]. He, [[Iliffe vector|John Iliffe]], Robert Futrelle,<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.ccs.neu.edu/home/futrelle/ |title=R.P. Futrelle, Biological Knowledge Laboratory, North Western University |access-date=22 February 2011 |archive-date=4 March 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304052856/http://www.ccs.neu.edu/home/futrelle/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> Paul Fehder, [[George Coulouris (computer scientist)|George Coulouris]] and other members of the CCL worked on [[parsing]],<ref>M.P. Barnett and R.P. Futrelle, "Syntactic analysis by digital computer", Communications of the Association for Computing Machinery, 5, pages 515–526, 1962</ref> text processing (the precursor of [[word processing]]),<ref>M.P. Barnett and K.L. Kelley, ''Editing verbal texts by digital computer'', American Documentation, 14, 99, 1963.</ref> programming language constructs,<ref>M J Bailey, M P Barnett and R P Futrelle, "Format free input in FORTRAN", Communications of the Association for Computing Machinery, 6, 505, 1963.</ref> [[scientific visualisation]],<ref>I.G. Csizmadia, B.T. Sutcliffe and M.P. Barnett, ''A group orbital treatment of lithium hydride'', Canadian Journal Chemistry, 42, pages 1645–1663, 1964.</ref> and further topics that melded into the computer science of later years.

==Institute of Computer Science==
In 1963, Barnett accepted an appointment as reader in information processing at the [[Institute of Computer Science]] in the [[University of London]],<ref>[http://infotrac.galegroup.com/itw/infomark/119/327/139874238w16/purl=rc1_TTDA_0_CS102590030&dyn=40!xrn_51_0_CS102590030&hst_1?sw_aep=prin77918 ''British Scientist Leaving U.S.'', The Times, February 14, 1964, page 6, issue 55935, col. G.]</ref> and, while he was still at Massachusetts Institute of Technology, the [[Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (United Kingdom)|Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (DSIR)]] awarded him a grant, to be taken up in London, to continue his work on computer typesetting, that was publicised by the director, [[Buckingham potential|Richard A. Buckingham]].<ref>[http://infotrac.galegroup.com/itw/infomark/119/327/139874238w16/purl=&dyn=sig!10?sw_aep=prin77918 ''Towards Printing by Computer'', The Times, February 22, 1964, page 6, issue 55942, col. E]></ref> His return received further publicity as a "reverse brain drain".<ref>''Scientist Back From U.S.: New Light Cast on '"Brain Drain"'', The Times, 25 March 1964, page 10, issue 55969, col. G.</ref><ref name="guardian1964">[https://www.proquest.com/docview/184852130 ''Automated Printing at Universities'', The Guardian 26 March 1964, page 9].</ref> He worked extensively with printing trade union officials and the staff of training colleges, to provide understanding of the new methods and their potential (pages 208–218 of his book).<ref name=mitPress /> His concern with social aspects of technological innovation is noted in a detailed book review.<ref>John Seybold, American Documentation, 17 (4) 219, 1964.</ref> He served on the Information Committee of the [[Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (New Zealand)|DSIR]].<ref>M P Barnett, ''The information explosion'', Nature, 203, 585, 1964.</ref>

Asked about university research in England, in a BBC interview on his arrival in 1964, he said "the trouble was deeper than money ... Frustration is caused by concentration of power in the hands of a few."<ref>"Reversing Current Tide, British Scientist Returns", The New York Times, 25 March 1964, page 18.</ref> His deepening concern about entrepreneurial activity in academe intensified, (Section 10.6 of his book.<ref name=mitPress />)

==Industry, Columbia and CUNY==
After a year at the Institute of Computer Science, Barnett went back to the US He joined the newly formed Graphic Systems Division of [[RCA Corporation|RCA]], to create software for commercial computer typesetting. RCA acquired the US rights to the Digiset machine of [[Rudolf Hell]] and marketed an adaptation as the Videocomp. About 50 were sold.<ref>Jack Belzer, Albert G. Holzman and [[Allen Kent]], ''Encyclopedia of computer science and technology'', volume 5, page 350.</ref> Barnett designed the algorithmic markup language PAGE-1 to express complicated formats in full page composition.<ref>John. Pierson, Computer composition using PAGE-1, Wiley Interscience, New York, 1972.</ref> This was used for a wide range of typeset products that included, over the years, the ''Social Sciences Index'' of the [[H. W. Wilson Company]] and several other publications excerpted in a later review paper.,<ref name=educom>M P Barnett, ''Electronic publishing for educational institutions'', in D. D. Mebane (ed.), ''Solving college and university problems through technology'', pages 121—158, EDUCOM, Princeton, New Jersey, 1981.</ref> The application to database publishing led Barnett to devise and implement a programming language, that he called SNAP, to express file handling operations as sequences of grammatical English sentences.<ref>{{Citation |publisher = Harcourt, Brace & World |location = New York |author = Michael P. Barnett |title = Computer programming in English |date = 1969 |ol = 5754250M }}</ref>

In 1969, Barnett joined the [[H. W. Wilson Company]], a publisher of bibliographic tools for libraries, to automate the production of these. He designed and introduced the system that was used to produce the ''Social Sciences Index'' for about 10 years. He had also started to teach courses on library automation at the Columbia School of Library Service.<ref>M P Barnett, ''Computer hardware and software for librarians'', in P.J. Fasana and A. Veaner (eds.), ''Collaborative library systems development'', MIT Press, Cambridge, Massachusetts, 1971.</ref> He joined the Columbia faculty full-time in 1975.

In 1977, Barnett moved to the Department of Computer and Information Science at [[Brooklyn College]] of the [[City University of New York]] in 1977, retiring as professor emeritus in 1996. Whilst at CUNY, he directed a major NSF funded project to develop computer generated printed matter for undergraduate teaching.<ref name=educom /> He wrote software that incorporated pictures in documents that were typeset using PAGE-1.<ref name=educom /> He wrote several books with his three teenage children, Gabrielle, Simon and Graham, aimed at the home market. These dealt with the production of computer graphics on early personal computers, that included the [[Commodore 64]],<ref>{{Citation |publisher = Reston Publishing Co. |isbn = 0-8359-0454-7 |location = Reston, Va |title = Beginning graphics for the Commodore 64 |author = Michael P Barnett and Gabrielle R Barnett |date = 1985 |id = 0835904547 |ol = 2849295M}}</ref> the [[Apple II]],<ref>{{Citation |publisher = Little, Brown |isbn = 0-316-08164-7 |location = Boston |title = Personal graphics for profit and pleasure on the AppleÆ II Plus computer |author = Michael P. Barnett and Graham K Barnett |date = 1983 |id = 0316081647 |ol = 3493113M}}</ref> and [[IBM PC]],<ref name=ibmpc>{{Citation |publisher = Little, Brown |isbn = 0-316-08220-1 |location = Boston |title = Personal graphics for profit and pleasure on the IBM personal computers |author = Michael P. Barnett and Graham K Barnett |date = 1984 |id = 0316082201 |ol = 21267624M}}</ref> and the use of elementary [[algorithms]].<ref>{{Citation |publisher = McGraw-Hill |isbn = 0-07-003792-2 |location = New York |title = Animated algorithms |author = Michael P Barnett and Simon J Barnett |date = 1986 |id = 0070037922 |ol = 2547803M |url-access = registration |url = https://archive.org/details/animatedalgorith0000barn}}</ref> <!--He and his wife, Barbara, used Page-1 and his pictorial typesetting software to produce the PC graphics book.-->

==Integrals redux, retirement and symbolic calculation==
In 1989, Barnett started to spend part of his time as a visiting scientist at the John von Neumann National Supercomputer Center,<ref>''Science on the ETA10'', John von Neumann National Supercomputer Center, Consortium for Scientific Computing, 1988.</ref><ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=gJMrAAAAYAAJ&dq=john+von+neumann+supercomputer+center&pg=PA14 A R Hoffman and J F Traub, ''Supercomputers: directions in technology and applications'', National Academy Press, 1989.]</ref> located on the outskirts of Princeton and run by a consortium of universities. He restarted work on molecular integrals, using the power of the supercomputer to go beyond the possibilities of the 1960s. After his retirement from CUNY, he continued to explore applications of [[symbolic calculation]] to molecular integrals, [[nuclear magnetic resonance]], and other topics.<ref>[https://www.princeton.edu/~nmr/apseq/index.htm M P Barnett, ''Symbolic computation, Slater orbitals and nuclear magnetic resonance''.]</ref>
